details:
**Tess of the d'Urbervilles**
Hardy's most famous novel (1891), the near-universal giveaway. Tess Durbeyfield, a poor girl whose father learns the family descends from the noble d'Urbervilles, is seduced and raped by Alec, marries Angel Clare, and is finally hanged for murdering Alec. Hardy famously closes it by saying "the President of the Immortals" had "ended his sport with Tess."

**Angel Clare**
The parson's son who falls in love with Tess while she works as a milkmaid at Talbothays Dairy alongside Retty, Izz, and Marian. On their wedding night Tess confesses her past, and Angel abandons her and goes to Brazil; he returns too late, and at the end Tess asks him to marry her younger sister, Liza-Lu.

**Tess stabs Alec and is arrested at Stonehenge**
Tess kills Alec d'Urberville, the man who raped her, at a boarding house called The Herons in the resort town of Sandbourne. She flees with Angel and sleeps on the Stone of Sacrifice at Stonehenge, where she wakes to the police and says "I am ready." A black flag raised over the prison at Wintoncester signals her execution.

**Sorrow**
The name Tess gives the sickly baby born after Alec rapes her. She baptizes the dying infant herself because the vicar will not, and after its death she leaves home to work at Talbothays Dairy.

**The Mayor of Casterbridge and the sale for five guineas**
Hardy's 1886 novel opens at a country fair where a drunken Michael Henchard, after drinking furmity (a porridge) laced with rum, auctions his wife Susan and daughter Elizabeth-Jane to the sailor Newson for five guineas. Ashamed when he wakes, he swears not to drink for twenty-one years, and he later rises to become mayor of Casterbridge.

**Michael Henchard, Donald Farfrae, and Lucetta**
Henchard's rival is the Scottish corn merchant Donald Farfrae, who overtakes his business, marries his former lover Lucetta Le Sueur, and later marries Elizabeth-Jane, who turns out to be Newson's daughter. Lucetta dies after townspeople stage a "skimmity-ride" mocking her past affair, which Jopp exposes by reading her letters aloud. Henchard dies ruined, leaving a will asking "that no man remember me."

**Jude the Obscure**
Hardy's last novel (1895), about the stonemason Jude Fawley, who dreams of becoming a scholar at Christminster. He is tricked into marrying Arabella Donn and loves his cousin Sue Bridehead, who marries the schoolteacher Phillotson before living with Jude. The novel's harsh reception helped push Hardy to give up fiction for poetry.

**Little Father Time and "Done because we are too menny"**
Jude's son by Arabella, raised in Australia and sent to live with Jude and Sue. Told that the family is poor and that Sue is expecting another child, he hangs his half-siblings and then himself, leaving the misspelled note "Done because we are too menny."

**"The Convergence of the Twain"**
Hardy's poem on the 1912 sinking of the Titanic, subtitled "Lines on the loss of the 'Titanic'" and collected in Satires of Circumstance. It begins "In a solitude of the sea / Deep from human vanity," describes a "sea-worm" crawling "grotesque, slimed, dumb, indifferent" and "dim moon-eyed fishes" in the wreck, and says "the Immanent Will that stirs and urges everything" made a "Shape of Ice" grow as the ship grew.

**Far from the Madding Crowd**
An 1874 novel whose title comes from Thomas Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard." Gabriel Oak is ruined when his dog drives his sheep off a cliff and becomes a shepherd for the farmer Bathsheba Everdene. She sends the farmer William Boldwood a joking valentine that he takes seriously, and she marries the dashing Sergeant Frank Troy, who woos her with a sword exercise and had earlier jilted Fanny Robin after she went to the wrong church. Boldwood shoots Troy, and Bathsheba finally marries Gabriel.

**The Return of the Native**
An 1878 novel set on Egdon Heath that opens with Guy Fawkes Night bonfires. Clym Yeobright gives up his job as a diamond merchant in Paris and becomes a furze-cutter, to the dismay of his wife Eustacia Vye, who longs to escape to Paris and is drawn to Damon Wildeve. Eustacia and Wildeve drown in a weir, and the reddleman Diggory Venn marries Thomasin.

**"The Darkling Thrush"**
A poem dated December 31, 1900, beginning "I leant upon a coppice gate." The bleak landscape is "the Century's corpse outleant," the "ancient pulse of germ and birth" seems shrunken, and "tangled bine-stems" score the sky "like strings of broken lyres." An aged thrush suddenly "fling[s] his soul / Upon the growing gloom," suggesting "some blessed Hope, whereof he knew / And I was unaware."

**Wessex**
The fictional region of southwest England, based largely on Hardy's native Dorset, where most of his novels are set. Hardy revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom's name for it, and his major works are often called the Wessex novels.

**Prince and the "blighted star"**
Early in Tess, Tess falls asleep while driving a wagon of beehives to market, and the family's only horse, Prince, is killed in a collision with the mail cart. Just before, she tells her brother that they live on a "blighted" star rather than a sound one.

**A Pair of Blue Eyes**
An 1873 novel in which Elfride Swancourt is courted by the young architect Stephen Smith and later by the critic Henry Knight. A scene in which Knight is left hanging from a cliff, at the end of a serial installment, is often credited with giving rise to the term "cliffhanger."
